newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - DCP spending spree not over yet.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - DCP spending spree not over yet.

text.p: Listed New Zealand investor Direct Capital Partners has bought up large in recent weeks but the spending spree isn't over yet, Chief Executive Ross George said on Friday.
"We've got some really good prospects on our table at the moment," George told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"Our aim is to remain relatively fully invested while we have a positive view of the economy."
Earlier, DCP announced the latest in a string of recent investments which have seen it spend over NZ$71 million since its formation two and half years ago.

The NZ$7.5 million purchase of a 25 percent stake in South Island retirement village operator Ryman Healthcare comes just 10 days after DCP announced taking a 44.5 percent holding in airfreight and aviation group Airworks (NZ) for $12 million.
But George said DCP still had just under $20 million in cash reserves and was on the look-out for good investments.
"I would anticipate that we would have capacity to invest another $20 million," he said.
"The position with funds like ours is that you don't rush it, but you have to get to a level of investment that presents an appropriate risk reward profile, and diversity is a key part of that."
DCP has already established a diverse portfolio.
The company presently has shareholdings in nine New Zealand companies ranging from movie maker Communicado through to wine producer Nobilo.
George said DCP generally targeted younger companies with a high growth potential.

"We've generally invested in businesses that have got quite a desire to grow their business areas. When you invest with groups like that you're asking them to fulfil that growth aspiration, and in some instances obviously that costs money," he said.
"But if you're confident that they're doing the right thing, then a couple of years of building is very much worthwhile."
George said DCP had realised a $3.7 million gain on its $9.8 million investment in Blue Star, an actual return of 37 percent.

He said the sale in October of a 25 percent stake in PC Direct, which it bought for $4.16 million, was expected to reap over $7 million. And the company had sold about 83 percent of its shareholding in Sky City to realise $17 million. It spent $12.1 million on the initial investment.
George said DCP still had about 500,000 Sky City shares and had received stock in consideration for the PC Direct sale which it could easily liquidate for investment cash if the need arose.

He said DCP's profits were difficult to predict because it did not take controlling stakes in its investments, but the company aimed to grow its net tangible asset backing (NTA) by 13 percent annually.
"The main focus is on ensuring that our NTA growth continues. Shareholder wealth in the company is what we're trying to grow, rather than current year earnings," he said.
Last June DCP began repurchasing its own shares because it said they were trading at an inappropriately high discount to the asset backing, which it put at over 83 cents per share.

George said DCP had bought back about 2.24 percent of its total shares on issue at an average of about 71 cents a share, and although it was not currently in the market for its own stock, it would not rule out buying back more in the future.

"It's a tool that the board will always keep in mind in looking at the capital base. It's a really useful corporate tool to have, so yes, it is something that we'll keep under consideration," he said.
The shares were trading at NZ$0.75 on Friday, down a cent.
DCP had no intention of selling any of its businesses at present and George said New Zealand's currently positive economic climate was conducive to further investment.

"The (centre-right) coalition government are probably not going to manage the economy as tightly as it has been in the past, and obviously that's good for a domestic economy," he said. "As an investor in this country you've got to think the medium term looks reasonably positive, and I guess we do."
